mappings.note: False: 1, 4, 9, 16 has ratios 4, 2.25, 1.78, so the constant-ratio test of LO-11 fails. The item exists to make that test be applied rather than assumed.
Names the common ratio. LO-11 vocabulary, the GP counterpart of the common difference.
The formula n(n+1)/2 for the sum of the first n natural numbers -- C-11.1-LO-1 exactly. Not the general AP sum, which this chapter leaves to the competency.
Applies the formula to n=50 and explains the pairing argument behind it. LO-1's 'derives the sum of the first n natural numbers'.
Why n(n+1)/2 is always an integer: one of two consecutive numbers is even. A property of the LO-1 formula rather than of progressions generally.
The 1-to-100 case, worked both by formula and by pairing. Same LO-1 outcome as qid:706873 with a different n.
The full reverse-and-add proof of n(n+1)/2. LO-1's derivation clause, at five marks.
The sum of two consecutive triangular numbers is a perfect square -- a property of the triangular numbers, which LO-1 ties to the sum of the first n naturals.
Lists 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 and identifies each as a running total of the naturals. LO-1's 'relates the result to the triangular numbers'.
Proves algebraically what qid:706877 states, using T(n) = n(n+1)/2 twice. LO-1, with the formula supplied by the same outcome it is used to extend.
The fourth triangular number is 10. LO-1's triangular-number clause, as a gap-fill.
Dot patterns plus the two-copies-make-a-rectangle argument. That is the visual derivation of n(n+1)/2 that LO-1 names.
Each term is the sum of the two before it -- the recursion itself, which LO-9 names for the Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence. No cultural context is asked for, so not C-11.1-LO-2.
The answer is explicitly about Virahanka counting rhythms of Sanskrit metre, which is C-11.1-LO-2; the recursion that makes it work is LO-9. Both halves carry the three marks.

What makes a figure a fractal: the same rule repeated at every scale, i.e. self-similarity. C-11.1-LO-3 is the only outcome in this frame that deals with figures 'built by repeating one rule', and self-similarity is that principle stated generally.

Contrasts a fractal with an ordinary figure, which stops having structure when magnified. Cited to LO-3 for the same reason as qid:706884 -- it is the chapter's only fractal outcome, and the repeated rule is its mechanism.
LO-3 in full: the construction by removing middle triangles, and then the progressions in the count and in the area. The perimeter discussion is the same outcome pushed one step further.
What an explicit formula gives -- any term straight from its position. LO-8's definition; the contrast with a recursive rule is not drawn here, so not LO-9.
Derives 4n+1 from the constant difference 4 (LO-10) and then uses it to jump straight to the 20th term (LO-8). The item asks for the formula first, which is why LO-8 leads.
The recursive-versus-explicit contrast, which needs both outcomes: LO-9 defines the recursive form and LO-8 the explicit one. Neither alone describes what is assessed.

Both forms are written for 3, 6, 12, 24 -- the recursion (LO-9) and 3 times 2^(n-1) (LO-8) -- and getting there requires recognising the common ratio 2 (LO-11). The judgement about when each form is useful rests on all three.
The assertion is false because a recursion needs its initial terms: exactly the point LO-9 makes in generating Virahanka-Fibonacci from a recursion plus two seeds.
Fifth term of the GP 2, 6, 18 from a times r^(n-1). LO-11's nth-term formula, applied directly.

Doubling bacteria modelled as a GP, evaluated at h=8 and then inverted to find when the count first exceeds 100000. LO-11's formula used forwards and backwards; the growth is multiplicative, so LO-10 does not apply.
The count of shaded triangles after three stages is 3^3 -- LO-3's 'geometric progression in the number of its parts', with the number rather than the area.
The shaded area shrinks by a factor of 3/4 each stage and so tends to zero. LO-3's area progression, the counterpart of qid:706894's count.
Draws the first three stages and tabulates both the count and the area at each, so it exercises both progressions LO-3 names in a single construction.
